meta.title: Why it's wrong to look at work-life balance as an achievement

paragraphs.text: Few topics have been so endlessly analysed as work-life balance. The quest to attain this mysterious state has dominated discussion around careers for years—especially for working parents. The concept is often presented as something to achieve, or a goal to reach. And once you've reached it, congratulations: you've made it; you're a successful human being of the 21st century.

paragraphs.text: And, according to new findings, it may not be. Some researchers are now encouraging us to stop thinking about work-life balance as an achievement that you either hit or don't. Instead, they suggest it may be more of a lifelong process—a continuous, never-ending exercise that requires self-awareness and timely adjustments. Researchers Ioana Lupu and Mayra Ruiz-Castro argue that work-life balance is "a cycle, not an achievement". In their 2020 study, the researchers interviewed nearly 80 employees at two London-based firms—an equal number of men and women between the ages of 30 and 50, all with at least one dependent child—who worked in middle or senior management roles.

paragraphs.text: Lupu and Ruiz-Castro identified five steps that the respondents in the study who had better work-life balance used in their jobs. First, they paused and reconsidered beliefs such as "I'm a professional, so I should work, work, work", and asked themselves questions like, "What's currently causing me stress?" Second, after identifying the cause, they zeroed in on their resultant emotions. Did they feel angry, sad, energised? Third, they reprioritised, asking "Is working long hours really worth cutting back on family time?", for example. Fourth, they considered their alternatives: is there anything at work that could be changed to accommodate these new priorities? And finally, they implemented changes, like asking their supervisor for greater flexibility, or deciding not to take on every project that comes their way.

phrases.usage: 注意区分：increasing（不断增加的）/ increased（增加了的）/ increasingly（越来越）。常见搭配：increasing numbers / increasingly（注意区分）。
phrases.example: An increasing number of firms offer leave. 越来越多的公司提供休假。

phrases.meaning: 满足、满意
phrases.usage: 注意区分：satisfaction（满意、满足，不可数）/ to one's satisfaction（令某人满意的是）/ satisfactory（令人满意的，指结果达标）/ satisfied（感到满意的，指人）/ satisfying（令人满足的，指事）/ dissatisfaction（不满）。常见搭配：instant satisfaction / to one's satisfaction。
phrases.example: She smiled with satisfaction. 她满意地笑了。

phrases.meaning: 给、提供；举办、作（出）；让步、塌下（give up 放弃）（give 的现在分词/动名词形式）
phrases.usage: 注意区分：giving（现在分词/动名词）/ give（原形）。
phrases.example: All of this was done in the name of increasing job satisfaction and giving workers greater flexibility, and to assure workers that it was something management was committed to. 做这些，名义上是提满意度、给弹性，其实也是想让员工知道：公司是真承诺了，不是走过场。

pitfalls: 被动语态的过去分词不能误写成过去式；不及物动词没有被动。
注意区分：increasing（不断增加的）/ increased（增加了的）/ increasingly（越来越）。
注意区分：satisfaction（满意、满足，不可数）/ to one's satisfaction（令某人满意的是）/ satisfactory（令人满意的，指结果达标）/ satisfied（感到满意的，指人）/ satisfying（令人满足的，指事）/ dissatisfaction（不满）。
analysis.paragraphRole: 点明措施的双重目的「提满意度／给弹性」与「让员工信」，把 J 段措施与第 37 题结果接起来。

sentences.text: Unsurprisingly, Kelly and Moen found that employees in the redesign group reported less stress and less burnout.

analysis.translationLiteral: 不出所料，Kelly 与 Moen 发现，重构组里的员工报告了更少的压力与更少的精疲力竭。
analysis.translationNatural: 结果毫不意外：改了管理那一组，压力和倦怠都明显更轻。
analysis.structMarkup: (Unsurprisingly), 【Kelly and Moen】 _found_ {that employees in the redesign group reported less stress and less burnout}.
analysis.structureSummary: 主谓 + 宾语从句（that 引导）+ 评注性状语

components.note: 评注整句，暗示结果顺着前文措施而来
两位研究者并列
后接 that 从句给出发现

phrases.meaning: 不出所料地、不足为奇地、果然
phrases.usage: 注意区分：unsurprisingly（不出所料地，常置句首修饰整句）/ surprisingly（令人惊讶地，反义）/ unsurprising（不意外的）/ predictably（可预见地，近义）。
phrases.example: Unsurprisingly, Kelly and Moen found that employees in the redesign group reported less stress and less burnout. 结果毫不意外：改了管理那一组，压力和倦怠都明显更轻。

phrases.meaning: find 的过去式与过去分词（发现）；另作独立动词「创建、创办」
phrases.usage: 注意区分：found（find 的过去式）/ find（原形）/ founded（创建，独立动词的过去式）。常见搭配：found that... / be found to be。

phrases.meaning: 雇员、员工、受雇者（employee 的复数）
phrases.usage: 注意区分：employee（雇员，-ee 被…的人）/ employer（雇主，-er 施动者）/ employ（动词）/ employment（就业）/ -ee 与 -er 方向相反，同类 interviewer/interviewee。

analysis.structMarkup: 【They】 _were less likely to quit their jobs_; (indeed), (over the next four years), they were _40% less likely to quit_ (than those who kept working under the old policies).

phrases.meaning: 可能的；很可能（be likely to do）
phrases.usage: 注意区分：likely（可作 adj./adv.）/ probable/possible（只作形容词）。常见搭配：be likely to do / more likely than。

phrases.meaning: 确实、的确（加强语气）；甚至
phrases.usage: 注意区分：indeed（确实）/ really（真的）/ actually（实际上）。常见搭配：indeed, ... / very ... indeed。

phrases.meaning: 年、年份；岁数、年纪（year 的复数）
phrases.usage: 注意区分：year（年，可数）/ for years（好多年，与完成时连用）/ in a year's time（一年后）/ a five-year-old（复合词中 year 不用复数）/ ear（耳朵，拼写易混）。
phrases.example: They were less likely to quit their jobs; indeed, over the next four years, they were 40% less likely to quit than those who kept working under the old policies. 这组人更不容易走；往后四年，离职率比沿用老规矩那批低了整整四成。

paragraphs.text: "Work-life balance is understood to be an individual's response, so people think 'it's up to me to manage the craziness of my work life'", says Kelly. But organisations need to examine the demands they're placing on employees. "The root problem is not how the two pieces of work and life come together. It's that we have unrealistic expectations of what we're asked to do on the work side." If your workplace isn't an environment where work-life balance is possible in the first place, any effort you attempt to make toward it on a personal level will be in vain.

phrases.example: But organisations need to examine the demands they're placing on employees. 可公司该反过来查查：自己到底给员工压了多大的担子。

注意区分：need to do（实义动词）/ need do（情态动词，多用于否定疑问）。
